articles.summary: A New York father is struggling to arrange his five-year-old daughter’s funeral after the child was found dead at their Queens home, with the girl’s
articles.body: A New York father is struggling to arrange his five-year-old daughter’s funeral after the child was found dead at their Queens home, with the girl’s mother charged with murder after allegedly telling a 911 dispatcher, “I killed my daughter.”Kuldeep Singh has launched an online fundraiser to cover the funeral and cemetery expenses for his daughter, Fabiana Cabello, who was found unresponsive at the family’s home in South Richmond Hill, Queens, on October 14.“I loved my daughter very much, and losing her feels like I lost my whole world,” Singh wrote on the fundraising page, explaining that the funeral home and cemetery were asking for a deposit he could not afford.The grieving father said he was trying to continue working as an Uber driver while coping with the loss, but the emotional strain and funeral costs had made the situation difficult.“I am trying to keep working as an Uber driver while driving a rental car, but I am grieving and struggling to manage these costs at the same time,” he wrote, appealing for donations to give Fabiana a proper funeral and burial.Mother allegedly called 911 and confessedFabiana’s mother, Francis Cabello, 32, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder in connection with the child’s death.Police said officers responded to a home in South Richmond Hill at around 6.55 pm on October 14 following an emergency call. They found Fabiana unresponsive and took her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead.Although police did not publicly identify the caller, law enforcement sources told multiple news outlets that Francis made the call and allegedly told the dispatcher, “I killed my daughter.”According to a criminal complaint obtained by People, investigators believe the incident occurred between 5.30 pm and 6.55 pm that day.Fabiana was found with scrapes on her face and petechiae — tiny spots caused by bleeding beneath the skin — in her eyes, heart and lungs, according to the complaint. These findings can be associated with asphyxia. The medical examiner is responsible for determining the official cause of death.Francis was arraigned on October 16. She did not enter a plea and was due to return to court on October 20, according to the Queens District Attorney’s Office. She was also taken to a hospital for a psychiatric evaluation, according to reports.Family devastated by child’s deathThe tragedy has left Fabiana’s family struggling to come to terms with her death while her father seeks financial help to lay her to rest.The child’s uncle remembered her as a joyful girl who brought happiness to the family.“She’s a very beautiful girl, you know,” he told NBC New York, describing how she made her grandparents happy and gave family members warm hugs.Fabiana’s grandfather, Franklin Cabello, also spoke of the family’s devastation.“As a family, we feel mentally and physically destroyed,” he told reporters, adding that they were placing their confidence in God.Singh’s fundraiser asks people to contribute towards the funeral and cemetery costs or share the appeal with others. He said any donation would help ease the financial burden during one of the most difficult periods of his life.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A “gracious” trial court and a “very indulgent” Allahabad HC paved the way for two offenders in a grievous hurt case to go scotfree without
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A “gracious” trial court and a “very indulgent” Allahabad HC paved the way for two offenders in a grievous hurt case to go scotfree without spending a day in jail on the grounds that they suffered because of a 22-year-long trial, but the courts did not consider the victim, who is still getting treatment, Supreme Court has said.Now, SC has directed the accused in the 2003 case to surrender and asked the HC to conduct a fresh hearing.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said it was a case of misplaced sympathy. The trial court had awarded fiveyear jail terms to the two, but the HC released them on probation. SC said the case was “doomed from its inception insofar as justice delivery to the victim is concerned”.“We cannot but, with an amount of consternation, notice the casual manner in which the trial court and the high court considered the issue from the stage of taking cognisance till the release of the accused on application of Probation of Offenders Act. They have gone scot-free without suffering a single day of imprisonment, especially by reason of the misplaced sympathy based on grandiose expositions of law,” it said.The court passed the order on an appeal filed by the brother of the victim, who has lost substantial functionality of both upper limbs.SC said the HC “went overboard” and wondered how it could pass such an order despite the adverse report on the character of the offenders, noting that theywere involved in multiple criminal cases. “True, protracted trial is agonising but here, the accused were on bail and merrily indulging in criminal activities,” the bench said. articles.title: India & United States to boost defence, energy ties, Marco Rubio says trade deal close
articles.summary: Foreign Minister S Jaishankar met his US counterpart Marco Rubio in Mumbai, agreeing to further expand cooperation in energy, defence and technology ties
articles.body: Foreign Minister S Jaishankar met his US counterpart Marco Rubio in Mumbai, agreeing to further expand cooperation in energy, defence and technology ties and committing to an early conclusion of the trade deal still under discussion.While Rubio emphasised the role that the US can play in the diversification of India’s energy and defence supplies, Jaishankar said in a post on X that they also discussed people-to-people ties, alluding to India’s concerns over immigration and H-1B governance issues. Speaking at the US anniversary celebrations later, Jaishankar said in Rubio’s presence that Indian talent and skills have helped shape the tech era in the US.The ministers met ahead of a likely meeting between PM Modi and President Donald Trump next month on the margins of the Asean summit in Manila, and also before Modi’s visit to the US in December for the G20 meet.A State Department readout said Jaishankar and Rubio discussed regional and global issues, including developments in West Asia.Only a small number of items left to wrap up: Rubio on Indo-US dealRubio reiterated that increased energy trade with the US could play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizeable consumer demand.Rubio’s second visit to India comes against the backdrop of the US’s Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which is intended to penalise countries purchasing Russian oil, and Trump’s subsequent temporary suspension of related tariffs. India maintains that its oil procurement is essential not only for its own energy security but also for the stability of global markets. Rubio lauded the “substantial progress” made by India in diversifying its energy portfolio.Rubio also focused on reducing India’s reliance on Russia for defence supplies, stressing the deepening of defence interoperability and framing increased Indian purchases of US technology as a win-win situation for both countries.According to the US readout, Rubio also commended recent progress in bilateral defence and civil nuclear cooperation and advocated increased purchases of US technologies and systems that could enhance the security and prosperity of both countries.In a post on X, Rubio said he and Jaishankar had reaffirmed the importance of advancing the US-India strategic partnership. The ministers will meet again on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta later this month. Both will also join their counterparts from Japan and Australia for a meeting of the Quad foreign ministers in Atlanta.According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Jaishankar and Rubio welcomed progress in negotiations on the India-US bilateral trade agreement and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion.Rubio said the two sides were “as close as you can be without having an executed agreement”.“I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up… and hopefully have some good news to announce fairly soon, and perhaps the leaders can sign it thereafter,” Rubio told travelling US media.Shortly after arriving in Mumbai, Rubio laid a wreath at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel to honour the victims of the 26/11 terror attacks.“Secretary Rubio underscored the Trump administration’s commitment to dismantling terrorist networks and ensuring that those responsible for acts of terrorism are brought to justice, including individuals facing charges for their roles in planning the 2008 Mumbai attacks,” the US State Department said, without naming Pakistan.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court has set aside a Central Information Commission order directing the Indian Air Force to disclose flight records pertaining to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi high court has set aside a Central Information Commission order directing the Indian Air Force to disclose flight records pertaining to foreign visits undertaken by PM Narendra Modi and former PM Manmohan Singh, stating such disclosure could compromise national security and the PM’s safety.Allowing a petition by the Central Public Information Officer of Directorate of Personal Services, Air Headquarters, Justice Amit Mahajan held the IAF was justified in denying access to the records under section 8 of RTI that exempts disclosure of information that could jeopardise national security or pose a risk to a person’s life and physical safety.The high court said CIC erred in directing disclosure of Special Flight Returns (SFR-II) after redaction of the names and particulars of security personnel, observing removing such details would not necessarily eliminate the potential security risks.The RTI plea was filed by retired Commodore Lokesh K Batra in 2018, seeking information about foreign visits by Indian PMs on IAF aircraft from April 1, 2013, until the date of his application.In response, the IAF provided certain information about Modi’s foreign travels, and stated there had been no travel by ex-PM Singh on IAF aircraft during the period from April 1, 2013 to May 25, 2014. However, it refused to disclose copies of the SFR, Part-I and Part-II, citing national security concerns and the confidential nature of the records.Batra approached CIC, which directed the IAF on July 8, 2020, to provide certified copies of available and relevant SFR-II records to the applicant.The IAF challenged the CIC order, contending the records contained sensitive information that could potentially enable the identification of security personnel, reveal the composition of PM’s entourage and allow inferences to be drawn about patterns of security deployment.Justice Mahajan said, “The mere fact that public funds have been expended on the foreign visits of the PM does not, by itself, justify disclosure of information which may compromise the security arrangements put in place for such visits.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump says Russia 'has been fine on Ukraine' as he makes new deals with Putin. Will his strategy pay off?
articles.summary: The president insists that his latest moves will end the war and lower prices for Americans. Experts aren't so sure.
articles.body:
A series of Trump administration moves over the last two weeks — including decisions to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and delay other measures targeting the Russian economy — have led both Republicans and Democrats to question whether President Trump is changing course and siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the war between their two countries.

"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump told reporters on Monday. "They haven't been doing much."

In contrast, the president continued, "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that."

Russia and Ukraine have been at war for more than 12 years. But in February 2022, the conflict entered a new, deadlier phase when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and tried to seize territory. The fighting has since become a grinding war of attrition. The United States has generally supported Ukraine, even as direct military aid has waned during Trump's second term .

The administration's latest steps, however, "amount to a major reversal in U.S. strategy," the New York Times reported on Sunday . "The breach with Ukraine has been sudden and perhaps irreparable."

So what's going on here? Posting Sunday on social media , Trump defended his actions by insisting that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" and doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine, he said, is targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which is "hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." He said that "farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World."

But even Republicans have pushed back. "I think it's clear Russia is the aggressor, and we've got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia," GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida told the Associated Press over the weekend. "So it's not the first thing I would be doing."

When Zelensky was asked last week if he believed Ukraine was "losing" the U.S., he replied: "Yes."

"It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," Zelensky said.

On Tuesday, Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo , Norway. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, participated via video link. On Wednesday, Witkoff and Kushner will reportedly fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Putin in his hometown with "an updated set of [peace] proposals," according to the BBC.

Is a diplomatic breakthrough in the offing? Here's what you need to know about the latest developments.

Oct. 9: Trump said he had reached an agreement with Putin to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets. Minutes later, the Treasury Department announced that it would be lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027. Those sanctions — which limited Putin's ability to bankroll the invasion of Ukraine — have been in place since 2022.

"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" the president wrote on social media.

Oct. 10: Trump blamed Zelensky for high U.S. diesel prices and said Ukraine should replace him. "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump told reporters before leaving for a campaign rally in Tennessee . "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does."

Oct. 11: On social media, Trump declared an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine." He claimed that "both parties have agreed." Zelensky said the agreement was news to him , but added that he would be willing to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries if Russia pauses attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and other energy infrastructure in return.

Oct. 11-14: For three days, Zelensky held his fire on Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Putin continued to bombard Ukraine's energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power ahead of winter. The Trump administration clarified that its "energy ceasefire" applied solely to attacks on oil refineries , but Ukraine doesn't have any fully operational oil refineries — Russia has repeatedly attacked and disabled the last one in recent years.

Oct. 14: Ukraine discovered that its access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network — as well as Starshield, its military-grade counterpart — had been throttled , limiting its ability to defend itself from Russian ballistic missile attacks on energy infrastructure. "Right at the moment Trump was warning Zelensky not to attack Russian refineries, the Starshield settings were somehow altered, such that the system could not track objects traveling at speeds greater than about 100 miles per hour — woefully inadequate to detect Russian aerial assaults," the National Review explained .

Citing four sources familiar with the discussions, the Telegraph reported that "Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine" and that Trump "agreed." In response, Trump denied any involvement, saying, "I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon." Musk wrote on social media that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."

Reuters also reported that the "order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside [the] White House." The Wall Street Journal reported this week that "Elon Musk ordered the slowdown" — "a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration."

Oct. 15: Zelensky said that Ukraine would resume attacking Russian oil refineries. "That's it," Zelensky told the Financial Times . "The block is out. We're done."

Oct. 16: Trump issued an executive order waiving new sanctions against Russia — as well as tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy — that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act that he signed in September. "I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," Trump told Newsmax . "I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin."

Oct. 18: Trump wrote on social media that his "decision on Russia is a very simple one" aimed at striking a peace deal and lowering energy costs for Americans.

"Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," Trump claimed, saying that he doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."

He continued, "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way."

In contrast, Trump claimed Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

Oct. 19: Citing "a U.S. official and three additional people familiar with the situation," the Washington Post reported that the Trump administration is holding up "the transfer of interceptor missiles to Ukraine that are needed to protect the country from Russian missile and drone attacks."

Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky again, saying, "It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

Oct. 20: Witkoff and Kushner met with Zelensky in Oslo. According to the BBC , Zelensky suggested after the meeting that "crucial issues of early warning of Russia's ballistic missile strikes had… been resolved." Zelensky also said that he discussed Ukraine's access to missiles and Starlink with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio — and he expected "good results."

Will Trump's deals with Putin lower U.S. diesel prices?

Trump has accused Zelensky of "knowing that these attacks" on Russian refineries "are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States."

It's true that the price of diesel is up about 77% so far this year — putting it near record highs and raising costs for American farmers, truckers and businesses (which in turn puts upward pressure on the price of consumer goods and services).

But energy analysts say the Iran War, not Ukrainian attacks on Russia, is the major reason diesel is so much more expensive than it used to be. "The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz, that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," one recently told the New York Times .

In 2025, Russian diesel exports accounted for roughly 9% of the global diesel trade — or about 700,000 barrels a day, according to S&P Global Energy. That number has fallen to about 140,000 barrels a day since Ukraine started targeting Russian oil refineries.

Trump's deal with Putin would amount to another 75,000 barrels a day, according to the New York Times .

That's not nothing — but experts say it's also not enough to make a huge price difference in the U.S. To put those 75,000 barrels in perspective, diesel exports from Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries have fallen by 800,000 barrels per day since the start of the Iran war in February.

Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, estimated in an Oct. 9 social media post that Trump's deal with Russia could eventually lower the cost of diesel by 10 to 20 cents per gallon. Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, likened the impact to "putting a Band-Aid on a gunshot wound."

And that's assuming Russia can deliver. According to the Times, "many analysts consider [even] those numbers to be unrealistic because roughly 40 to 50 percent of Russian refining capacity is offline" — and "repairing and restarting refineries can take months or years in the best of circumstances."

Trump has been taking various steps to try to lower U.S. gas prices ahead of November's midterm elections, including signing an executive order allowing tax-free purchases of red-dyed off-road diesel. But an October AP poll found that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of how the president is handling the cost of living — and 65% now blame his policies for persistently high prices more than factors beyond his control.

Will Trump's deals with Putin end the war?

On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright described Trump's diesel deal as a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine.

It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC News .

The Times has also reported that the "Trump administration's talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner."

"The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia's biggest energy companies," the paper added.

Meanwhile, at their talks in Oslo on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner were expected to tell Zelensky that "holding out to retain occupied portions of the country's eastern provinces is not worth it — and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia's terms," according to the Times .

In short, the Trump administration appears to be pushing harder than ever before to force Ukraine to cede sovereign territory to Russia as part of a negotiated end to the war.

Whether Zelensky succumbs to that pressure remains to be seen. "I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," he told Bloomberg in an interview published on Sunday . "I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."

"If the United States will support Putin — it's unbelievable, it's a tragedy," Zelensky added Sunday on NBC News's Meet the Press . "If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand."

articles.title: Drone strike on a market in disputed African region of Abyei kills at least 153
articles.summary: A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, hit a nearby fuel depot, killing at least 153 people and igniting a fire that was still burning Tuesday, a local official said.
articles.body: A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, hit a nearby fuel depot, killing at least 153 people and igniting a fire that was still burning Tuesday, a local official said. Yohanna Akol Ngor, the Abyei administration’s caretaker information minister, blamed Sudan’s military for Monday’s attack on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town. “We have recorded 153 deaths,” Ngor told the Associated Press by phone Tuesday. He said the death toll continued to rise as the fire burned. A senior Sudanese military officer said the army carried out a drone strike Monday targeting fuel tankers arriving from South Sudan that he said were bound for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The officer said those killed were RSF members and people involved in fuel smuggling. “We do not target civilians,” he said. The AP could not independently verify his account of the targets or the identities of those killed. The officer said the strike took place outside the demilitarized zone along the border with South Sudan. Doctors Without Borders, known by its French abbreviation MSF, said more than 20 wounded people were brought to Ameth Bek Hospital, where MSF teams were working alongside staff from South Sudan’s Health Ministry. “So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted,” said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF’s medical activities manager at the hospital. South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry also blamed Sudan’s military, saying the attack hit multiple locations within the market, causing civilian casualties and extensive property damage. The ministry said it summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to “refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property.” It called for issues concerning Abyei to be addressed through diplomatic channels. Sudan’s military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have been fighting since April 2023, devastating large parts of the country and threatening stability along its borders. Ngor said the strike hit around 11 a.m. Monday. He said the fuel depot supplied local businesses. “It is a horrible and shocking situation,” he said. MSF called on all parties to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, expressing concern about people’s ability to safely reach healthcare and other essential services. Amiet Market is a trading hub serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities. The oil-rich Abyei region’s status was left unresolved by a 2005 peace agreement that ended decades of civil war, and it remained unsettled when South Sudan became independent in 2011. A proposed referendum stalled over disagreements about who could vote. The region’s majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan. Abyei has also experienced deadly communal violence, including fighting over land between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities.

articles.summary: Rubio tells US media that reaching a peace deal with Tehran is extremely difficult while Hormuz attacks continue.
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio tells US media that reaching a peace deal with Iran is extremely difficult and economic pressure will continue until Tehran stops targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi tells the media the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, adding that indirect talks continue through Pakistan and Qatar.

articles.title: Why former FDLR fighters are returning to Rwanda
articles.summary: From the forest to Mutobo, former fighters face the challenge of rebuilding their lives after leaving the armed group.
articles.body:
Musanze, Rwanda – Jean Claude Hategekimana feared that returning to Rwanda could cost him his life. After years with the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), he decided to leave the armed group and return home. At Rwanda’s Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre, he began preparing for civilian life.

Born in 1996 in Rutsiro District, in western Rwanda, Hategekimana moved to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his parents and grew up in an area controlled by the FDLR. He joined the group in 2018, underwent military training and eventually reached the rank of captain.

“I arrived at the Mutobo Centre after fighting to defend Goma. Following our defeat, I fled to Masisi. After realising that I was fighting for nothing, I decided to return to Rwanda. I came back on February 24,” he told Al Jazeera.

Hategekimana said FDLR members had been taught that anyone who returned to Rwanda would be killed.

“Upon arriving in Rwanda, I realised that the FDLR had been lying to us. For me, returning home felt like embarking on a suicide mission,” he said.

His experience illustrates the challenge of reintegrating former fighters whose beliefs and fears have been shaped by years in an armed group.

Francis Musoni, secretary-general of the Rwanda Demobilisation and Reintegration Commission, said the Mutobo centre, located in Musanze in Rwanda’s Northern Province, was established in 2001 to receive members of the FDLR and other Rwandan armed groups returning from the DRC.

The FDLR emerged in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsis. After the genocide, members of the former Rwandan armed forces and militia groups fled to what was then Zaire, now the DRC. The Rwandan government accuses the FDLR of carrying out attacks against Rwanda and contributing to cross-border insecurity.

At Mutobo, the rehabilitation programme includes medical care, psychosocial support, civic education and assistance with reconnecting with families. Returnees can also contact relatives and friends through a telephone service, Musoni said.

“We help them to build confidence among themselves, build trust, and empower them to go back into the community and contribute to the development of the country together with their families,” he said.

The centre also allows visitors and media representatives to meet returnees. Musoni said those undergoing rehabilitation can visit their communities for short periods to help rebuild their confidence in returning home.

“They can travel to their communities [during rehabilitation]. They are given written permission for a week or two, and we even facilitate transport,” he said.

For the former commanders interviewed by Al Jazeera at Mutobo, the decision to leave the FDLR was shaped by family ties, disillusionment and concerns about personal safety.

Major-General Anastase Munyaneza served in the former Rwandan armed forces in Kigali’s Kicukiro District during the 1994 genocide. He said he left Rwanda after the genocide and later joined the FDLR, eventually commanding its South Kivu sector.

Although he had come to accept the group’s beliefs, Munyaneza remained in contact with his family in Rwanda. News of their lives made him question his own circumstances.

“I was the only one who had fled to the DRC. I regularly received news about them. I knew they were still alive, attending school, working for the government and improving their lives. I began asking myself what I was doing in the forest,” he said.

He added that seeing other members return safely encouraged him to consider going home.

Munyaneza said he contacted personnel from the United Nations Organisation Stabilisation Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), who transported him from South Kivu to Bukavu and then to the Congolese-Rwandan border. He subsequently proceeded to Mutobo.

Lieutenant-Colonel Idrissa Bizimana, who was responsible for ideology, propaganda and recruitment within the FDLR, said his decision to return followed a change in his convictions.

“I no longer believed in the ideology I had been promoting. After receiving verified information about what was happening in Rwanda, I decided to return home,” he said.

Bizimana said he had been in contact with a MONUSCO general who had offered to help him return. Using a satellite phone equipped with GPS, he sent his location and the date. A helicopter was then dispatched to retrieve him, he said.

Lieutenant-Colonel Emilien Mpakaniye, who joined the FDLR in 1998 and was responsible for economic affairs at its headquarters, said he began questioning the organisation after becoming disillusioned with what he described as its lies.

Colonel Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR intelligence commander, returned to Rwanda in 2022 and underwent rehabilitation at Mutobo. He said he decided to leave after another commander accused him of working with Rwanda following a disagreement over a mission in Bujumbura.

Nshimiyimana said the accusation made him fear for his life.

“When they accuse you of working with Rwanda, it means they consider you a Tutsi, and the next step is to kill you,” he said.

At Mutobo, former fighters receive education and practical support to prepare for life after discharge.

Febronie Mukankiko, a teacher at the centre, said teaching people who grew up in the forest required a different approach.

“Our students are different from ordinary students. They are adults who grew up in the forest, so teaching them requires special skills. We undergo additional training to ensure that we can teach them effectively,” she said.

She added that completing their studies could be a significant achievement for those with limited access to formal education.

“When they graduate and receive their certificates, they are very happy,” she said.

Musoni said the average stay at the centre was five months, after which returnees completed a formal discharge process. He said assistance could include financial support, vocational training, formal education and help establishing income-generating activities. The commission also follows up with former residents to assess how they are adjusting to life in their communities.

For those who have spent years away from Rwanda, leaving Mutobo marks the start of another transition: finding work, reconnecting with family and adjusting to civilian society.

For Mpakaniye, disillusionment came partly from the contrast between the lives of senior commanders’ families and those of ordinary fighters.

“First, their family members live in Rwanda and in Europe, while ours are in the forest,” he said.
